catalog_quote: The basic foot type in Limilngan is the trochee. In general, polysyllabic morphemes constitute independent stress domains and feet are aligned from the left edge of these morphologically determined domains. Monosyllabic or consonantal suffixes are incorporated into the preceding domain. ... Consequently, all disyllabic words have an initial stress, regardless of their internal morphological structure. [p.32] The majority of trisyllabic uninflected words also bear stress on their first syllable. The other trisyllables bear stress on the second syllable. The appearance of penultimate stress in trisyllables is not random, but rather shows a relationship to syllable weight. Trisyllables with a heavy second syllable are likely to show penultimate stress. As vowel length is not contrastive in Limilngan, syllable weight depends solely on the nature of the coda. new_statements.rule_in_words: Trochaic feet built left-to-right from the left edge of each polysyllabic morpheme (the stress domain); monosyllabic/consonantal suffixes join the preceding domain; final syllables are not stressed; where a word has several stresses the LAST (rightmost) stress is primary (verbs p.35: 'The final stress is the primary stress'; quadrisyllabic nouns: secondary on 1st, primary on 3rd). Default outcome: initial stress in disyllables and most trisyllables; but heavy syllables (coda clusters, and codas that are laterals, taps, continuants or hetero-organic nasals — not homorganic nasals, geminate halves or most stop codas; vowel length is not contrastive) attract stress, giving penultimate stress in trisyllables with a heavy 2nd syllable; comparative vowel sonority is a further, weaker factor. Monosyllabic prefix complexes are unstressed before polysyllabic roots but stressed before monosyllabic roots; polysyllabic prefix complexes take a secondary stress on their first syllable. A few verb paradigms ('get', 'give', 'hit') have irregular stress on the pre-root syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly described: perceptible primary vs secondary distinction (primary = greatest amplitude); alternate syllables after the first stressed syllable of the root carry stress; polysyllabic prefix complexes carry secondary stress on their initial syllable; in quadrisyllables secondary on 1st syllable, primary on 3rd; words with three stresses are common but no secondary/tertiary ranking among non-primary stresses.
new_statements.exceptions: Trisyllables with heavy (cluster/sonorant-coda) 2nd syllable take penult stress (8 of 9 with coda clusters; 4 of 4 with lateral/tap/continuant coda; 4 of 7 with hetero-organic nasal coda; only 2 of 12 with hetero-organic stop coda); eight open-syllable trisyllables with unexplained penult stress (e.g. uwagi 'fire', luwarli 'rat'), possibly vowel sonority; quadrisyllables 'less predictable'; irregular pre-root stress in paradigms of 'get' and disyllabic-prefix + monosyllabic-verb words ('give', 'hit'); word-level suffixes and reduplication/compounds form their own stress domains (2.6.3-2.6.4).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress, described over morphologically defined domains (root+root-level suffixes vs prefixes vs word-level suffixes); based on the speech of the last fluent speaker (Felix Holmes); amplitude is the main perceptual cue, vowel length uncertain, tone stated to be phrase-level not word-level (5.1, Appendix A). Author compares the system to Larrakia's quantity-sensitive trochees with final-foot primary stress, noting Limilngan's coda-sonorancy sensitivity is less consistent.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Limilngan proper (glottocode nucl1327 'Nuclear Limilngan', ISO lmc), recorded from the last fluent speaker Felix Holmes in the Mary River region; not Wulna. No dialect differentiation described.
